summary: AI design partner for custom silicon and end-to-end chip verification.
editor_note: A chip-design claim gets more interesting when the hardware runs a workload. Architect Labs reports Redwood Nano running Qwen3-0.6B on an FPGA, with RTL, verification, and software generated from a human specification. Unlike an EDA plug-in, it sells a design partnership across the program. Its ASIC efficiency figures are projections, not measured production silicon; tapeout and independent replication remain the harder tests.

sources.label: Redwood FPGA demonstration and ASIC projection boundaries
Architect Labs Redwood preprint abstract, version 2

product_evidence.claim: Architect Labs describes partnering with chip companies and workload owners on custom ASIC programs, spanning architecture, RTL, verification, physical design, and tapeout rather than selling a standalone EDA tool.

The Redwood preprint reports generating a performance model, RTL, UVM environments, formal proofs, firmware, and kernels from two architects' high-level specification in under two weeks; this is the company's reported demonstration.

The August Redwood post reports a 2x2-tile Nano design on an AMD Versal VPK180 FPGA at 250 MHz, running Qwen3-0.6B at 12.1 tokens per second. These are company-reported FPGA measurements, not a fabricated ASIC result.

The same post labels its Samsung 8 nm performance-per-watt comparison as an ASIC projection and says full GDSII and a TSMC tapeout are further work. It does not establish volume production of Redwood silicon.

market_context.primary_user: Semiconductor companies and workload owners, including AI labs and physical-AI teams, seeking a partner for an existing ASIC program or a new custom-chip design.
market_context.differentiation: Its proposed unit of work is the chip program: human architects specify a workload while an integrated system generates and checks hardware and software artifacts together, instead of optimizing one EDA step.
market_context.why_now: The August Redwood disclosure adds an inspectable FPGA demonstration and a technical preprint to the earlier design-partner proposition, while explicitly leaving ASIC realization as further work.

risks.claim: FPGA inference and process-node projections do not establish ASIC power, yield, timing closure, or production readiness. The reviewed disclosure leaves GDSII completion and a TSMC tapeout ahead.
risks.basis: VentureDex assessment of the Redwood post and company-authored preprint abstract; no independent replication or foundry acceptance evidence reviewed.

risks.claim: The public materials do not disclose named customer tapeout results, contract pricing, or how much expert work each engagement requires. A single demonstrated design does not establish repeatability across ASIC programs.
risks.basis: VentureDex assessment of the design-partner offer and published demonstration; no customer contracts, design files, or product trial reviewed.
